newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries close sharply lower amid worries.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries close sharply lower amid worries.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities closed sharply lower on Friday as investors' worries about renewed economic growth increased.

Yields on the 30-year bond rose to 6.66 percent at one point in the trading session, the highest since the closing level on July 2. Concern about a strong retail sales report next week and a weakening dollar contributed to bearish sentiment.
The Treasury's 30-year bond was closing down 1-1/2 points to yield 6.64 percent.
James Glassman, senior economist with Chase Securities Inc, said technicians had been talking about a selloff for a while, but discounted the impact of just retail sales.
"One report is not going to change your view (on the overall direction of the economy," Glassman said.
Inventories were growing at a phenomenal rate as businesses were responding to stronger consumer demand, but he saw that demand slowing in the fall and winter.
"The dollar is still up 12.5 percent on a trade-weighted basis with out major trading partners," despite recent weakening, Glassman said.
"To begin with, we had over optimism in the bond market, assuming economic growth moderating and the Federal Reserve not tightening," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp.
The dollar also had been appreciating, attracting foreign investors to Treasuries, "but that optimism has turned on a dime," Sohn said.

While most analysts had seen little prospect of the Fed raising interest rates at its August meeting, Sohn said the likelihood of the FOMC voting to further tighten monetary policy was probably now 50-50.
Treasuries were dragged down on Friday as investors feared a strong retail sales report next Wednesday could drive interest rates higher.
Producer prices and consumer prices also were due next week, but analysts retail sales would be the most watched barometer on what direction the economy was taking.

"The market's getting nervous about retail sales. We'll probably see a decent bounce, but the Fed won't move (to tighten monetary policy) until September," said Tom O'Neil, chief economist at Bank of Montreal.
O'Neil said there was no fundamental reason for the bond market's fall off on Friday, though there were some stories of diminishing Japanese buying of U.S. Treasuries early in the session.
"It's not a stampede, but a moderate correction," O'Neil said.
Meanwhile, the September bond contract broke through support at 113-07 to end at 112-21.
"There's no doubt that worry/caution is creeping back into the market" after weeks of large gains and market optimism," said O'Neil

At the short end of the maturity spectrum, three-month bills were one basis point lower at 5.15 percent. Six-month bills were unchanged at 5.23 percent and year bills were up six basis points higher at 5.29 percent.
The 10-year issue was 30/32 lower at 98-06 to yield 6.37 percent. The five-year was 12/32 lower at 99-2/32 to yield 6.22 percent and the two-year 5/32 lower to yield 6.01 percent.
